quote: But that was the best time of my life, and only now that it has gone from me forever—only now do I realize it.
source: Natalia Ginzburg, The Little Virtues, Winter in the Abruzzi, the closing sentence (trans. Dick Davis, 1985)

evidence.where: Salon's authorised reprint of the whole essay in Dick Davis's translation, fetched this run. The last sentence of the essay reads exactly as proposed, with 'forever' set as one word and the dash closed up, and Dick Davis is credited as translator.
evidence.edition: Dick Davis's translation of Le piccole virtu, first published in English as The Little Virtues by Carcanet Press in 1985; the text consulted is the Arcade Publishing reissue of that same translation, 2017
evidence.locator: Winter in the Abruzzi, the closing sentence, following the sentence about believing in a simple and happy future

reason: The wording, the translator and the position as the essay's last sentence all hold, and the typography was the thing worth checking: the Davis text has one-word 'forever' and an unspaced em dash, not the British 'for ever', so the proposal is right as it stands. The translation year is given as 1985, the first English publication of Davis's version, though the copy read was the 2017 reissue of that same translation. The essay's surrounding matter concerns her husband's death in prison, but the quoted sentence carries none of it and needs no warning. Natalia Ginzburg stands once already in the year, in month 5, so this is her second of three.
